docs.title: Operating Systems — CPU Scheduling & Deadlock
docs.text: CPU scheduling is the method by which the operating system decides which ready process runs on the CPU next. The scheduler aims to maximise CPU utilisation and throughput while minimising waiting time and response time. First-Come First-Served scheduling runs processes in the order they arrive and can cause the convoy effect when a long process blocks short ones. Shortest Job First scheduling picks the process with the smallest next CPU burst and gives the minimum average waiting time, but it can starve long processes. Round Robin scheduling gives each process a fixed time quantum and then moves it to the back of the ready queue, which makes it suitable for time-sharing systems. A very large quantum makes Round Robin behave like First-Come First-Served, while a very small quantum wastes time on context switches. Priority scheduling serves the process with the highest priority first, and aging gradually raises the priority of waiting processes to prevent starvation. A deadlock occurs when a set of processes are each waiting for a resource held by another process in the set. Deadlock requires four conditions together: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait. Deadlock prevention breaks at least one of these four conditions, while deadlock avoidance uses algorithms such as the Banker's algorithm to keep the system in a safe state. A safe state is a state in which the system can allocate resources to every process in some order and still avoid deadlock. A context switch is the act of saving the state of the running process and loading the state of the next one, and it is pure overhead because no useful work is done during it.

docs.title: Thermodynamics — Laws & Entropy
docs.text: Thermodynamics is the branch of physics that deals with heat, work and energy transfer between systems. The zeroth law states that if two systems are each in thermal equilibrium with a third system, they are in thermal equilibrium with each other. The first law states that energy can be neither created nor destroyed, so the change in internal energy of a system equals the heat added minus the work done by the system. The second law states that the entropy of an isolated system never decreases, which gives a direction to natural processes. Entropy is a measure of the disorder or the number of microscopic arrangements of a system. A Carnot engine is an ideal reversible heat engine that operates between two temperatures and has the maximum possible efficiency. The efficiency of a Carnot engine depends only on the absolute temperatures of the hot and cold reservoirs. An isothermal process occurs at constant temperature, whereas an adiabatic process occurs with no heat exchange with the surroundings. Enthalpy is the sum of the internal energy of a system and the product of its pressure and volume.
